questionText: Select the wrongly spelt word out of the four alternatives.
solution:

The other words - Excellence, Traitor, and Conscience - are all spelt correctly.

• Excellence: The quality of being outstanding (उत्कृष्टता)
• Traitor: A person who betrays his country or friends (गद्दार / देशद्रोही)
• Conscience: The inner sense of right and wrong (अंतरात्मा / विवेक)
conceptTested: Identification of standard English spelling rules and common orthographic errors (religious vs religeous).

questionText:
From the given options, select the homonym that corresponds to both Definition (P) and Definition (Q).
(P) The process by which a cell or molecule absorbs and integrates an external substance into its own physical structure

(Q) The legal process of officially forming and registering a new corporation or business entity
solution:
Meaning: The term Incorporation refers biologically/physically to combining or taking in something as part of a whole, and legally to the formation and registration of a corporate entity.

Assimilation applies only to biological or cultural absorption, not corporate registration.

Calcination and Acquisition do not satisfy both definitions.

Vocab Meanings: • Incorporation: Including something as part of a whole; forming a legal company (समावेशन / निगमन - कंपनी का पंजीकरण)
• Assimilation: Absorbing and integrating something (आत्मसात्करण / समावेश)
• Calcination: Heating a substance to a high temperature (निस्तापन)
• Acquisition: Buying or obtaining something (अधिग्रहण)
conceptTested: Identification of a single precise term corresponding to multiple contextual definitions across disciplines.

subject: English
questionText:
Read the following sentence and ascertain whether the underlined idiom is used correctly. If the usage is incorrect, choose the correct option (A/B/C) to suitably replace it. If the usage is correct, choose Option D: "No correction required."'

The evolutionary biologist expected his radical paper on genetic editing to spark a civil debate, but upon publication, he was forced to rule the roost as peers from every major research institute unleashed a barrage of harsh critiques, public reprimands, and demands for its retraction.
solution:
Meaning: To run the gauntlet means to undergo a severe ordeal, trial, or endure a barrage of criticism and hostile attacks from all sides.

The biologist faced "a barrage of harsh critiques, public reprimands, and demands for retraction.".

"To rule the roost" incorrectly means to dominate or be in control, making option (B) the proper replacement.

Vocab Meanings: • Run the gauntlet: To face severe criticism or attack from many sides (चारों ओर से आलोचना या हमले का सामना करना)
• Rule the roost: To be in charge; to dominate (वर्चस्व रखना / हुक्म चलाना)
• Drop the ball: To make a mistake (गलती करना / चूक जाना)
• The die is cast: A decision has been made that cannot be changed (निर्णय हो चुका / पासा फेंका जा चुका)
conceptTested: Idiomatic appropriateness and contextual application in complex prose.

questionText:
Read the sentence below carefully. Choose the option (A/B/C) that best improves the sentence. If the sentence is already correct, select Option D (No improvement required).

The institutional review board concluded that the gene-editing trial was not an insignificant breakthrough, though it was not entirely risk-free either.

options.A: It was the institutional review board's conclusion that the gene-editing trial, though not being an insignificant breakthrough, it was not entirely risk-free either.
options.B: The institutional review board concluded that the gene-editing trial was either not entirely risk-free but not an insignificant breakthrough.
options.C: The proposed gene-editing trial was concluded by the institutional review board to be neither an insignificant breakthrough and not entirely risk-free either.
options.a: It was the institutional review board's conclusion that the gene-editing trial, though not being an insignificant breakthrough, it was not entirely risk-free either.
options.b: The institutional review board concluded that the gene-editing trial was either not entirely risk-free but not an insignificant breakthrough.
options.c: The proposed gene-editing trial was concluded by the institutional review board to be neither an insignificant breakthrough and not entirely risk-free either.

solution:
Rule: The original sentence is grammatically sound, concise, and stylistically balanced using litotes ("not an insignificant breakthrough") followed by a coherent concessive clause ("though it was not entirely risk - free either").

Option (A) introduces a redundant subject pronoun ("it") creating a comma splice/run - on structure.

Option (B) incorrectly pairs "either" with "but".

Option (C) incorrectly pairs "neither" with "and not... either".

Therefore, no improvement is required.
conceptTested: Grammatical conciseness, stylistic balance, and avoidance of redundant structures or incorrect correlative conjunction pairs.

subject: English
questionText:
Find the grammatically sound direct speech representation of the indirect sentence from the options below.

Nandita told Abhay that if they had not hurried out of the room, they would not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for him to review.

options.A: Nandita told Abhay, "If we have not hurried out of the room, we will not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for you to have reviewed."
options.B: Nandita told Abhay, "If we have not hurried out of the room, we would not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for you to be reviewing."
options.C: Nandita told Abhay, "If we had not hurried out of the room, we will not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for you having reviewed."
options.D: Nandita told Abhay, "If we had not hurried out of the room, we would not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for you to review."
options.a: Nandita told Abhay, "If we have not hurried out of the room, we will not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for you to have reviewed."
options.b: Nandita told Abhay, "If we have not hurried out of the room, we would not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for you to be reviewing."
options.c: Nandita told Abhay, "If we had not hurried out of the room, we will not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for you having reviewed."
options.d: Nandita told Abhay, "If we had not hurried out of the room, we would not have come back so soon pushing those tall wire carts full of babies for you to review."

solution:
Rules: In third conditional sentences expressing an unreal past conditional ("If + past perfect, would have + past participle"), the tense of the conditional clause remains unchanged in indirect speech reporting.
Pronoun shifts: "they" converts back to "we", and the indirect objective pronoun "him" converts to "you".

The infinitive purpose phrase "for him to review" corresponds directly to "for you to review".

Thus, option (D) is the exact, grammatically correct direct speech form.
conceptTested: Backshift rules and pronoun adjustments for third conditional sentences in indirect to direct speech conversion.

subject: English
questionText:
In increasingly interdependent ecosystems, trust is no longer a soft virtue but a strategic asset that determines institutional resilience. While many organizations profess commitment to transparency, such declarations often fail to __ (A) under scrutiny when operational opacity persists beneath performative disclosure. Moreover, stakeholders are increasingly unwilling to __ (B) rhetorical assurances, particularly when prior breaches of confidence have not been adequately redressed. This skepticism is further amplified in digital environments where information asymmetry and rapid dissemination of partial narratives distort institutional intent. In such contexts, leaders must __ (C) reputational capital with caution, as overextension of goodwill may precipitate a rapid erosion of legitimacy. Nevertheless, trust deficits, once entrenched, do not easily __ (D) through cosmetic reforms or episodic outreach initiatives. Such dynamics underscore the importance of aligning formal governance structures with informal norms of accountability. Consequently, reputational repair requires sustained behavioral consistency rather than episodic signaling exercises that merely project responsiveness without substantive change. Therefore, institutions that consistently align incentives with ethical imperatives are more likely to __ (E) enduring legitimacy across shifting socio-political landscapes. Without such alignment, even well-designed frameworks risk gradual erosion of stakeholder confidence.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (A).
solution:
The idiom hold water means to remain valid, logical, or sound when examined or tested.

The passage states that declarations fail to hold water under scrutiny, indicating they cannot withstand examination.

Stand out means to be prominent, fall apart is contradicted by the preceding verb fail to, and break in means to enter forcefully.
conceptTested: Understanding contextual meanings of idioms and phrasal verbs in passages

solution:
To command legitimacy or respect means to elicit, secure, or hold it by virtue of one's actions and worth.

Institutions aligning ethical incentives are able to command enduring legitimacy.

Compromise (weaken or undermine), confine (restrict), and contest (dispute) contradict the positive outcome described in the concluding sentence.
